Definition: Affordability of mobile broadband data, measured as the cost of a basic mobile data plan (1-2GB) as a percentage of GNI per capita. The UN Broadband Commission target is below 2% of monthly GNI per capita. Affordability is the single largest barrier to internet adoption in Africa.
Comments: World Bank project document cites price of 1GB mobile broadband internet at 20.8% of GNI per capita (affordability report referenced in PAD).
revision_notes: The cited World Bank PAD source states a 2019 basket price of 20.8% of GNI per capita, but this specific figure could not be located in the accessible text of that document and is inconsistent with contemporaneous and subsequent independent data. The World Bank's own 2020 Cameroon Digital Economy Assessment records mobile broadband pricing of roughly 1.4-3.1% of GNI per capita (ITU/GSMA 2017-2019 data), and a 2025 synthesis citing Internet Society and World Bank IEG analysis puts the 2023 price of a 1GB mobile data bundle at 3.1-3.6% of GNI per capita (average USD 1.63/GB). This places Cameroon in the 'Moderate (2-5% GNI p.c.)' band, not 'Very Expensive'. Score revised from 1 to 3.
revised_comments: A basic 1GB mobile data bundle costs the equivalent of roughly 3.1-3.6% of monthly GNI per capita in Cameroon, with an average market price of about US$1.63 per GB (2023 data). This exceeds the UN Broadband Commission's 2% affordability target but sits within a moderate cost band, being cheaper in relative terms than several regional peers such as Ethiopia, Malawi and Chad, though still a barrier for lower-income users. High telecom taxation, including around 19% VAT plus excise duties, contributes to the retail price.

Definition: The country's total international internet bandwidth capacity per internet user, indicating the quality and capacity of the country's connection to the global internet. Determined by submarine cable landings (for coastal states), cross-border terrestrial fibre (for landlocked states), and satellite links.
Comments: International Internet bandwidth per Internet user reported as 1.8 kb/s (ITU data reproduced).
revision_notes: ITU-sourced data (reproduced via TheGlobalEconomy.com) shows international internet bandwidth per user of 1.8 kbit/s, the last year for which the ITU published a country figure for Cameroon (2016); a separate USAID mAccess diagnostic snapshot shows a similarly low figure of 2.55 kbit/s per user with no year specified. Both figures sit well within the 'Very Low (<5 kbit/s per user)' band. No more recent official ITU or World Bank figure for this indicator could be located for Cameroon despite searching; a 2022 World Bank report corroborates qualitatively that Cameroon underutilises its submarine cable capacity and has low international bandwidth per user relative to peers. Score of 1 confirmed, though the underlying data remain dated.
revised_comments: Cameroon's international internet bandwidth per internet user is very low by global standards, last measured by the ITU at around 1.8-2.6 kbit/s per user. Despite the presence of four submarine cable landings, a 2022 World Bank assessment finds the country underutilises this capacity - using only around 15-30% of the SAT-3/WASC and WACS cables - due to Camtel's monopoly over international gateway access, which keeps international bandwidth costs high and limits competitive expansion of capacity per user.

Definition: Whether the government has established dedicated data center infrastructure and/or a government cloud (G-Cloud) strategy for hosting e-government services and public sector data domestically. Critical for data sovereignty and e-government service delivery.
Comments: Huawei case study describes NSIF migration to modular data center and building a private cloud platform; Cameroon also pursuing 'sovereign cloud' with ST Digital.
revision_notes: The previously cited sources (a 2019 Huawei/NSIF case study and a 2025 article on ST Digital's role in the AI strategy) describe a private data centre and an AI strategy rather than a formal government data centre/cloud strategy. More current evidence supports the same code but on a stronger evidentiary basis: state-owned Camtel operates the Zamengoe Datacenter near Yaounde, publicly described in December 2025 as fully operational and used to host data for public administrations and businesses ('Camtel Cloud Days'). However, CENADI (the government's own computer services agency) only completed its three-year study of the national data centre ecosystem in May 2025, recommending policy measures on certification, security and connectivity - indicating no formal, adopted government cloud strategy yet exists. ANTIC stated in December 2025 that 80% of Cameroon-linked data remains hosted abroad. This supports 'Basic government data center operational' but not yet 'National data center operational with cloud strategy adopted', so the code is confirmed at 3.
revised_comments: The state-owned operator Camtel runs an operational data centre at Zamengoe, near Yaounde, which by December 2025 was being actively used to host data for government agencies and businesses as part of a national digital sovereignty push. A parallel government-led study by CENADI, completed in May 2025, mapped the country's data centre ecosystem and recommended measures on certification, security, connectivity and energy efficiency, but a formal, adopted national government cloud strategy has not yet been published; the national ICT agency ANTIC noted in December 2025 that around 80% of Cameroon-linked data is still hosted abroad.

Definition: Percentage of national population with access to electricity (grid or off-grid). This is the primary indicator of energy infrastructure availability for ICT. Based on World Bank/IEA Tracking SDG7 data, national statistical offices, or Afrobarometer surveys.
Comments: Electricity access rate reported as 71% (World Bank-statistics referenced in post; also echoed by World Bank feature).
revision_notes: The previous score of 4 (75-89%) was based on a Facebook post and a World Bank feature story; the feature story in fact itself states electricity access at 71% (2022/2023), which falls in the 50-74% band, not 75-89%. World Bank WDI data (EG.ELC.ACCS.ZS), corroborated by TheGlobalEconomy.com and other WDI-based aggregators, confirms national electricity access at 72.0% in 2023 (up from 71.0% in 2022). Score revised down from 4 to 3 to match the correct band.
revised_comments: National electricity access in Cameroon stood at 72% of the population in 2023, according to World Bank World Development Indicators data, up slightly from 71% in 2022. Access remains far from universal, with a pronounced urban-rural divide, and continued reliance on the Nachtigal Hydropower Plant and other new generation capacity to close the gap.

Definition: The gap between urban and rural electricity access rates. A smaller gap indicates more equitable energy distribution, critical for ensuring ICT infrastructure can serve the whole population, not just cities.
Comments: Urban access reported 95.8% (World Bank WDI via Trading Economics) and rural access estimated ~25% in World Bank video; gap ~71 percentage points (>60pp).
revision_notes: World Bank WDI data (via TradingEconomics) confirms urban electricity access at 95.8% and rural access at 26%, both for 2023, giving a gap of approximately 70 percentage points, within the '>60pp' band. This replaces the previous rural-access citation, which relied on a YouTube video rather than a primary statistical source; the WDI figures corroborate the same order of magnitude and support the same code. Score of 1 confirmed on stronger sourcing.
revised_comments: There is a wide urban-rural electrification gap in Cameroon: World Bank data show 95.8% of the urban population had access to electricity in 2023, compared with only around 26% of the rural population, a gap of roughly 70 percentage points. Rural electrification remains heavily dependent on extension of the interconnected grid and on mini-grid programmes under the national Rural Electrification Master Plan (PDER).

Definition: The gap between men and women in mobile internet usage or internet access. Based on the GSMA Mobile Gender Gap data or ITU gender-disaggregated ICT statistics. A smaller gap indicates more equitable access to digital opportunities.
Value Name: Very large gap (>40% fewer women online)
Comments: GSMA reports in Sub-Saharan Africa women were 36% less likely than men to use mobile internet (large gap proxy for Cameroon when country-specific not found).
revision_notes: No Cameroon-specific gender gap figure could be located from GSMA, ITU or Afrobarometer despite searching; Cameroon is not one of the survey countries in GSMA's Mobile Gender Gap consumer research and the national statistics office does not routinely publish sex-disaggregated ICT access data. The row therefore continues to rely on the Sub-Saharan Africa regional proxy used previously, updated to the latest available figure. Note also that the previous code of 1 (Very large gap, >40%) did not match its own cited evidence of a 36% regional gap, which itself falls in the 'Large gap (30-40%)' band. GSMA's Mobile Gender Gap Report 2026 (published June 2026, covering 2025 data) shows the Sub-Saharan Africa gender gap in mobile internet adoption has narrowed further to 26%, which falls in the 'Moderate gap (20-29%)' band. Score revised from 1 to 3 on a regional, not country-specific, proxy - flagged for review given the reliance on a proxy.
revised_comments: No Cameroon-specific data on the gender gap in mobile or internet access is published by GSMA, ITU or the national statistics office. As a regional proxy, GSMA's Mobile Gender Gap Report 2026 finds that women in Sub-Saharan Africa are 26% less likely than men to use mobile internet (2025 data), continuing a gradual narrowing of the gap from 36% in 2022. This places the region, and by proxy Cameroon, in a moderate gender-gap band, though country-specific verification is not available.
